Why Buy a NAS in 2026? The Case for Getting Off the Cloud

Here is the math that nobody puts in the headline.

A 2TB iCloud plan costs roughly $120 per year. If you have a family with an iPhone, an iPad, a Mac, and a few years of photos and videos, 2TB runs out faster than you expect. The next tier up is 6TB at $240 per year.

A home NAS setup with the Asustor Drivestor 4 Gen2 and three 12TB NAS-rated hard drives costs around $869 total upfront. That gives you a RAID 5 array with 24TB of usable, protected storage — twelve times what the 2TB iCloud plan provides. After the initial investment, your recurring storage cost is zero. No monthly bill, no data throttling, no terms-of-service changes, no questions about who can see your files.

The break-even point against a 2TB iCloud plan is roughly seven years. Against a larger cloud plan, it is much sooner. And unlike a cloud subscription, your NAS gets more capable over time as you add drives and the software improves.

Beyond the economics, there is the privacy argument. Every photo, document, and video you store on a home NAS stays on hardware you own, in a location you control. For a lot of people, especially those with professional work files or large personal media libraries, that matters independently of the cost.

The 2026 market has made this easier than it has ever been. Modern NAS devices are not the intimidating command-line projects they used to be. You set them up with an app. They back up your phone automatically, like iCloud does. They let you stream your media remotely, like a personal Netflix. If you have ever set up a Wi-Fi router, you can set up a modern NAS.

What to Look For in a Budget Home NAS

Before I get into the picks, here is what actually matters at this price point — and what does not.

Number of bays: This is the most important spec. A 2-bay NAS limits you to RAID 1 (mirroring), which means two drives give you the capacity of one. A 4-bay NAS opens up RAID 5, which gives you much better usable storage per dollar and allows one drive to fail without losing your data. If you plan to use this as a primary storage system for anything over a few terabytes, go 4-bay.

Networking speed: Most budget NAS devices ship with standard 1 Gigabit Ethernet, which caps real-world transfers at around 110 MB/s. That is fine for backups and streaming, but it becomes a bottleneck if you are moving large files regularly — RAW photos, 4K video footage, or large project folders. 2.5GbE roughly doubles that ceiling to around 280 MB/s. In 2026, with multi-gigabit routers increasingly common in homes, this is the spec worth paying for.

CPU and transcoding: For most home users, the ARM quad-core chips in budget NAS devices are more than sufficient for file serving, photo backup, and even Plex streaming when the files are pre-optimized. Where CPU matters more is on-the-fly transcoding — converting a 4K file to a lower resolution in real time for a device that cannot play the original format. AV1 hardware decode support, present in the newer Realtek RTD1619B chip, is a meaningful upgrade here.

Software: This is where Synology has historically dominated and why it still wins for pure beginners. But every major brand has improved significantly. The gap is narrower than it used to be.

What does not matter much at this price: M.2 SSD cache (nice to have, not transformative for home use), HDMI output (almost nobody uses this), and RAM expandability (1GB is enough for typical home workloads).

Software testing focused on the features most relevant to home users replacing a cloud subscription: automatic phone backup, photo management, remote access, and media streaming via Plex and Jellyfin. I tested 4K transcoding performance on devices with hardware acceleration claims, using high-bitrate files that would require real-time conversion rather than direct play.

Drive reliability and noise levels were monitored throughout each two-week period. Power draw was tracked using an energy monitor. Pricing was verified against current retail listings as of March 10, 2026, and reflects diskless (enclosure-only) costs unless otherwise noted.

Best Overall: Asustor Drivestor 4 Gen2 (AS1204T) — ~$269

This is the device that changed my recommendation in this category for 2026.

The original Drivestor 4 was already the best value 4-bay NAS you could buy. The result is 4K transcoding that is noticeably smoother than the previous generation — the kind of difference you actually feel when streaming a high-bitrate file through Jellyfin or Plex to a device that needs it converted on the fly.

The official lab figures show RAID 5 reads hitting 266 MB/s and writes around 160 MB/s over the 2.5GbE port. Slide the cover, slot the drives without touching a screwdriver, close it back up, and the ADM software walks you through the rest. I have set up a lot of NAS devices over the years, and this is the most frictionless first-boot experience I can recall outside of Synology's dedicated beginner products.

This model is actually made in Taiwan, and the attention to detail on the internals are incredible.

Day-to-day, the AS1204T runs whisper-quiet. At roughly 21 watts under load, it barely registers on an energy monitor. It sits on my desk, it does not make noise, and I forget it is there — which is exactly what you want from always-on home infrastructure.

The software, Asustor Data Master (ADM), has grown up considerably. Who should look elsewhere: Docker power users, anyone planning to run a media production workflow directly off the NAS, or anyone whose router and switch are still 1GbE (the 2.5GbE port would be wasted).

Head-to-Head Comparison

2-Bay vs 4-Bay: Which Should You Buy?

This is the most important decision in the under-$300 category, and most buyers default to 2-bay without thinking through the long-term implications.

Buy 2-bay if: Your storage needs are under 8TB total, you are a first-time NAS buyer focused primarily on phone backup and photo management, or you are price-sensitive and the DS223j's $189 is the ceiling.

Buy 4-bay if: You are building for the 12TB tier, you want to use RAID 5, or you want storage that scales without buying a new enclosure in two years.

Here is why RAID 5 changes the math significantly. With two 12TB drives in RAID 1, you get 12TB of usable space protected against one drive failure. Add a third 12TB drive to the Asustor AS1204T and switch to RAID 5, and you get 24TB of usable space — still protected against one drive failure. Add a fourth drive and you can move to RAID 6, which survives two simultaneous drive failures.

With a 2-bay NAS, none of that progression is possible. You are locked into RAID 1 from day one. When you outgrow it, you buy a new enclosure.

The Asustor AS1204T's 4-bay design is a one-time decision that gives you years of flexibility. At $80 more than a DS223j, it is an easy call for anyone who thinks they might need more than 8–10TB within the next few years.

RAID Explained Simply

RAID stands for Redundant Array of Independent Disks. In plain terms, it is how multiple drives work together to either protect your data, speed up access, or both.

For most home users building a 12TB setup, RAID 5 is the practical choice. It gives you the most usable space while keeping your data protected if a drive fails. When a drive dies — and eventually one will — you swap it out while the NAS keeps running, and the array rebuilds automatically.

One important note: RAID is not a backup. RAID protects against hardware failure, not accidental deletion, ransomware, or catastrophic events like fire or flood. For real data protection, follow the 3–2–1 rule: three copies of your data, on two different media types, with one copy off-site. Your NAS is two of those three. A cloud backup or external drive covers the third.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is an NAS under $300 a complete backup solution?

Mostly yes, but with one caveat. A home NAS replaces cloud storage effectively — automatic phone backups, photo management, Time Machine for Mac, file access from anywhere. What it does not replace on its own is off-site backup. If your home suffers a fire, flood, or theft, a NAS in that home is gone along with everything else. For full protection, pair your NAS with a cold backup to an external drive you keep somewhere else, or a low-cost cloud backup service for your most critical files.

Which NAS brand has the most user-friendly software for beginners?

Synology, and it is not particularly close. DiskStation Manager (DSM) is the benchmark the rest of the industry measures against. Synology Photos is intuitive enough for non-technical family members, and the onboarding process is the smoothest available. The trade-off is that Synology charges a premium for that software experience — their hardware is often more expensive for equivalent specs. Asustor's ADM has closed the gap considerably and is genuinely accessible for most users, but if you want the easiest possible experience above all else, Synology.

Can a NAS replace iCloud for photo backup?

Yes. Asustor's AiFoto 3 and Synology Photos both offer automatic phone backups, AI-powered organization, timeline views, and the ability to share albums with family members. The main practical difference from iCloud is that remote access requires a stable home internet connection and a decent upload speed. If you are on a slow broadband connection with limited upload bandwidth, streaming your own content back to yourself remotely can feel sluggish compared to a cloud CDN. For most home internet connections in 2026, this is not a problem.

Is a 2-bay or 4-bay NAS better for home use?

For long-term home use at the 12TB tier, 4-bay is significantly better. The ability to run RAID 5 means more usable storage per drive and protection against failure. With a 2-bay NAS in RAID 1, two 12TB drives give you 12TB of usable space. With a 4-bay NAS in RAID 5, three 12TB drives give you 24TB. The Asustor AS1204T at $269 costs $80 more than a DS223j but gives you four bays instead of two — that is the better long-term investment for anyone planning to store more than a few terabytes.

Can a budget NAS handle 4K streaming?

Yes, with the right hardware. The Asustor AS1204T's Realtek RTD1619B handles hardware-accelerated 4K transcoding including AV1 decode, which covers most modern streaming codecs. If your devices can direct-play the files — meaning Plex or Jellyfin does not need to convert them on the fly — even a less powerful NAS handles it without issue. Where you feel the CPU is when multiple streams need to be transcoded simultaneously or when a very high-bitrate file needs real-time conversion.

What are NAS-rated hard drives?

NAS-rated drives — like the Seagate IronWolf or WD Red Plus — are engineered for the specific demands of always-on NAS environments. They are built to handle continuous operation, the vibration of multiple spinning drives in an enclosure, and the higher workload cycles of a shared storage device. Standard desktop drives are rated for intermittent use and will typically fail faster in a NAS. The price premium over desktop drives is modest and worthwhile for any serious home setup.

How much does a home NAS cost to set up at 12TB?

A complete 12TB RAID 5 build using the Asustor AS1204T runs approximately $869: around $269 for the enclosure and $200 per drive for three 12TB NAS-rated hard drives. This gives you 24TB of usable storage with single-drive failure protection. After the initial investment, ongoing costs are essentially zero beyond electricity — roughly $2–3 per month at the AS1204T's 21W load.
